B10_00: Directed migration up a chemoattractant gradient is damped as well as driven. The brakes act at several levels: secreted cytokine-like mediators engaging their receptors, proteolytic processing of a complement component whose cleavage fragments are themselves chemoattractants and therefore a point of gradient control, a matrix metalloproteinase that limits recruitment, a signalling adaptor, and a surface immunoreceptor. A steroid-synthesising enzyme links hormone levels to response strength.
B10_01: Commitment along one differentiation programme is restrained rather than promoted here. The transcriptional arm includes a Runt-domain factor, a retinoic acid receptor and two zinc-finger factors that impose alternative programmes. Signalling and degradation components add further restraint: an inositol polyphosphate phosphatase dampens phosphoinositide-dependent growth factor responses, a pseudokinase directs turnover of lineage transcription factors, and a cullin supplies ubiquitin ligase activity, together setting the pace of lineage output.
B10_02: Release of preformed granule contents triggered by antigen crosslinking of a high-affinity immunoglobulin receptor is actively restrained. Part of the brake is applied at the membrane by surface immunoreceptors bearing tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, which recruit phosphatases to counter activating signals, and by lectin engagement of surface glycoproteins. Intracellularly, a Rab guanine nucleotide exchange factor restrains signalling downstream of receptor engagement, raising the threshold for exocytosis.
B10_03: Cytosolic double-stranded DNA sensing by a nucleotidyltransferase and its endoplasmic reticulum adaptor is braked at every step. Exonucleases degrade cytosolic DNA before it is sensed, the sensor is held in check by phosphorylation, acylation and tethering to chromatin, the cyclic dinucleotide second messenger is hydrolysed extracellularly, and adaptor turnover through autophagy and ubiquitin-ligase adaptors limits signalling duration. Phosphatase activity and damage-response proteins add further restraint.
B10_04: Activation triggered by antigen-antibody complexes is raised in threshold rather than initiated. The clearest mechanism is an inhibitory low-affinity immunoglobulin G receptor carrying a tyrosine-based inhibitory motif, which recruits phosphatases and so dampens activating receptor signalling. A neuropeptide acting through its own receptors provides a second brake, a heavily sialylated surface glycoprotein shapes adhesion and contact-dependent activation, and cytokine receptor signalling and endoplasmic reticulum stress handling contribute.
B10_05: Chemotactic movement across endothelium and through matrix is slowed by several distinct mechanisms. A secreted guidance ligand signals through Robo receptors to repel migrating cells and stabilise their cytoskeleton; a non-canonical receptor for a complement-derived fragment tempers signalling through the classical receptor for the same ligand; a secreted protein modifies hyaluronan-rich matrix to interfere with adhesion and transmigration; and a microRNA restrains the activation programme transcriptionally.
B10_06: Endosomal recognition of unmethylated CpG DNA by a Toll-like receptor, and the interferon and cytokine transcription it drives, are limited at distinct points. A surface immunoreceptor delivers an inhibitory signal that dampens interferon output, a small GTPase controls endosomal and lysosomal trafficking of the receptor and so limits its residence in the signalling compartment, and a receptor phosphatase and a lysosomal thioesterase further restrain downstream activation.
B10_07: Adhesion to endothelium and passage between endothelial cells is actively restrained. Chemokines pattern where migrating cells are held rather than recruited, so the same receptor signalling can retain instead of attract. A prostaglandin acting through one of its G-protein-coupled receptors raises cyclic AMP to suppress adhesion, a microRNA dampens NF-kappaB-driven transcription, and a phospholipase C isoform and a cytokine receptor subunit tune the conversion of chemotactic cues into firm arrest.
B10_08: Proliferation at an early developmental stage is damped by a combination of secreted morphogens and intrinsic cycle control. Bone morphogenetic protein and hedgehog family ligands released by neighbouring cells act on the dividing precursors to limit expansion, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor enforces cycle arrest, and a transmembrane regulator of Wnt responsiveness tempers proliferative signalling. Niche-derived cues and intracellular checkpoints therefore converge to balance proliferation against differentiation.
B10_09: Entry into this differentiation and fusion programme is held in check at several levels: a tight-junction claudin that alters systemic signalling, a secreted matrix glycoprotein that sequesters TGF-beta family ligands and so tunes how much differentiation signal precursors receive, an F-box substrate receptor that targets the lineage-determining transcription factors for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, an inhibitory immunoglobulin-like receptor that dampens ITAM-driven costimulation, and an iron-binding secreted protein that suppresses commitment.
B10_10: Commitment to this differentiation programme is actively opposed, keeping precursors proliferating and available for alternative fates. A cyclin-dependent kinase and a helix-loop-helix transcription factor sustain cycling rather than maturation, a homeobox factor and a zinc-finger factor impose alternative transcriptional programmes, an inositol polyphosphate phosphatase dampens signalling downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, and a microRNA tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally.
B10_11: Recognition of cytoplasmic double-stranded RNA by a DExD/H-box helicase sensor is braked at several points. A related helicase lacking the signalling domain competes with and modulates duplex RNA recognition; mitochondrial proteins restrain the outer-membrane adaptor; a RING-domain ligase ubiquitinates the sensor to drive its degradation; and cofactors of an AAA-ATPase segregase feed sensor and adaptor components into proteasomal turnover, setting the threshold and duration of signalling.
B10_12: Immunoglobulin output is capped by brakes at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors, including a sialic-acid-binding lectin and a low-affinity immunoglobulin G receptor, recruit phosphatases to raise the activation threshold and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while a complement receptor tunes complement-dependent stimulation. A BTB-domain repressor holds cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, an adaptor promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of responses, and cytokine receptor pairings add further restraint.
B10_13: Chemotactic recruitment along gradients is damped by several unrelated mechanisms: a decoy-like receptor for complement-derived anaphylatoxins tempers signalling through the classical receptor, a cell-surface peptidase trims chemokines and neuropeptides and alters their potency, a secreted guidance cue repels migrating cells, a hyaluronan-binding protein modifies matrix and limits transmigration, and a microRNA restrains the differentiation and activation programme itself.
B10_14: Commitment along this lineage programme is opposed rather than driven. A helix-loop-helix inhibitor sequesters E-protein transcription factors that would otherwise activate the programme, activin and inhibin subunits provide TGF-beta family signals that suppress differentiation, a secreted frizzled-related protein dampens Wnt signalling in the surrounding niche, and an HMG-box protein holds precursors in a less committed state. A complement receptor links the pathway to immune complex feedback.
B10_15: Cytokine output is damped at two levels. Intracellularly, a catalytically inactive decoy kinase occupies the Toll-like receptor signalling complex and blocks downstream NF-kappaB activation, and a CUE-domain protein dampens inflammatory transcription. Extracellularly, three TGF-beta ligands act through their receptors in autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory gene expression and shift the transcriptional programme toward a reparative, suppressive one, setting the threshold and duration of activation.
B10_16: Signalling by a type II interferon through its receptor is terminated and opposed at several points. A phosphatase dephosphorylates the receptor-associated JAK kinases and their STAT substrate to shut the cascade down; nuclear receptors, including two sterol-activated receptors and a fatty-acid-activated one, transcriptionally oppose interferon-induced gene programmes; a macrodomain ADP-ribosyltransferase biases signalling toward an alternative STAT; and an arginine hydrolase consumes the substrate nitric oxide synthase would otherwise use.
B10_17: Assembly of this sensor-adaptor-caspase platform is restrained at several levels. Ubiquitin ligases target the sensor for degradation, autophagy machinery including chaperone-mediated autophagy clears it, pyrin-domain-only proteins act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases, kinases and an NAD-dependent deacetylase tune the sensor through reversible lipid and other post-translational modification. Related NLR and pyrin-domain proteins and an inhibitory surface receptor add further input.
B10_18: Differentiation into the suppressive programme is opposed by several converging routes. A TNF-family ligand signals to responder cells and counteracts induction of the programme, checkpoint receptors and an interferon regulatory factor shape the cytokine and costimulatory environment in which the lineage-specifying forkhead factor is or is not induced, a secreted growth factor skews differentiation toward alternative fates, and microRNAs tune the same decision; proteasomal degradation of lineage factors contributes.
B10_19: Motility is reduced by signals acting at the surface and inside the cell. One early activation glycoprotein appears at the membrane and blocks egress by interfering with the receptor that senses a lipid gradient, while a surface ligand engaging its inhibitory receptor delivers a negative signal between neighbouring cells. Intracellularly, two Rho-family effectors dampen GTPase signalling, weakening chemokine-driven adhesion and polarisation so receptor input no longer produces movement.
B10_20: This differentiation programme is actively restrained by cytokine and receptor mechanisms. A heterodimeric cytokine signalling through a receptor that shares a common subunit limits the programme and promotes a regulatory one; a checkpoint receptor engaged by a beta-galactoside-binding lectin triggers exhaustion or death of effector cells; a soluble binding protein sequesters an interleukin that would otherwise amplify interferon output; and another interleukin skews responses toward an alternative programme.
B10_21: Interferon signalling is limited at the level of its triggers and its transducers. A cytosolic exonuclease and a dNTP triphosphohydrolase remove self nucleic acids before they are sensed, and adenosine deamination of double-stranded RNA marks endogenous duplexes as self. Downstream, a protease removes ubiquitin-like conjugates and blocks receptor-kinase engagement, a phosphatase dephosphorylates JAK-STAT components, and m6A-dependent decay, deadenylation and cap-binding translational repression shorten transcript life.
B10_22: Progression along this differentiation programme is held back by brakes at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors bearing tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs, including an immunoglobulin G receptor, a C-type lectin and a leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor, recruit phosphatases that dampen activating signals, and a non-classical MHC class I molecule serves as ligand for such receptors. Two related membrane proteins act intracellularly to hold cells immature, and a zinc-finger transcription factor limits activation.
B10_23: Commitment to this differentiation programme is actively opposed. Transcriptional restraint comes from a zinc-finger factor that sustains earlier progenitor programmes and from another that enforces an alternative lineage programme. Secreted inhibin and activin subunits and a secreted adipokine act on precursors from outside to dampen differentiation, while an RNA-binding protein and a tyrosine phosphatase that limits cytokine receptor signalling provide post-transcriptional and signalling-level brakes.
B10_24: Directed migration along chemokine gradients is damped by activities working at different levels. Secreted matricellular proteins and BMP antagonists act in the extracellular milieu; a repulsive guidance ligand signals through Robo receptors to block directed movement; a dual-specificity phosphatase dephosphorylates MAP kinases and so cuts short inflammatory signalling; and a surface immunoreceptor tempers activating responses. The brake is applied to the migratory response itself rather than to chemokine production.
